A1.name: robots.txt is reachable
A1.why: Crawlers look for robots.txt first; a server error here can block all of them at once.
A1.fix: Serve a robots.txt at your root that returns HTTP 200, even a minimal one.

A2.name: AI crawlers are allowed
A2.why: If AI crawlers are disallowed, assistants simply can't read or cite your pages.
A2.fix: Remove blanket Disallow rules for AI agents, or add explicit allow groups for the bots you want.
A2.code:
User-agent: GPTBot
Allow: /

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Allow: /

User-agent: PerplexityBot
Allow: /

A3.name: Homepage responds over HTTPS
A3.why: AI crawlers expect a working, secure homepage returning HTTP 200 over HTTPS.
A3.fix: Make sure the homepage loads over https:// and returns 200, with http redirecting to https.

B1.name: llms.txt file
B1.why: llms.txt is an emerging standard that tells AI models what your site is about and what to read.
B1.fix: Add a plain-text /llms.txt describing your site and linking its key pages.
B1.code:
# Your Company
> One-line description of what you do.

## Key pages
- https://example.com/: Homepage
- https://example.com/about: About us
- https://example.com/docs: Documentation

B2.name: sitemap.xml
B2.why: A sitemap helps crawlers discover all your pages instead of only the ones they stumble upon.
B2.fix: Publish a valid /sitemap.xml and reference it from robots.txt with a Sitemap: line.

C1.name: JSON-LD structured data
C1.why: Structured data lets AI understand the entities on your page with far less guessing.
C1.fix: Add a <script type="application/ld+json"> block with schema.org data to your pages.

C2.name: Useful schema types
C2.why: Types like Organization, Product or FAQPage map directly to what assistants answer.
C2.fix: Use schema.org types that fit your content: Organization, WebSite, Product, Article or FAQPage.

C3.name: Open Graph tags
C3.why: Open Graph gives a clean title, description and image when your page is shared or previewed.
C3.fix: Add og:title, og:description and (ideally) og:image meta tags in the head.

D1.name: Title tag
D1.why: The title is often the headline an assistant shows and reasons about.
D1.fix: Write a descriptive <title> of roughly 30–65 characters.

D2.name: Meta description
D2.why: A good description is a ready-made summary for AI answers and search snippets.
D2.fix: Add a meta description of roughly 70–160 characters.

D3.name: Single H1
D3.why: One clear H1 tells crawlers the main topic of the page.
D3.fix: Use exactly one <h1> as the page's main heading.

D4.name: Language & canonical
D4.why: lang helps AI answer in the right language; canonical avoids duplicate-content confusion.
D4.fix: Set <html lang="…"> and a <link rel="canonical"> on your pages.

D5.name: Homepage text volume
D5.why: If the homepage renders mostly via JavaScript, crawlers may see an almost empty page.
D5.fix: Make sure meaningful text (300+ words) is in the served HTML, not only after JavaScript runs.

D6.name: Question-answer format
D6.why: Q&A headings and FAQ blocks match how people actually ask assistants questions.
D6.fix: Add question-style headings or an FAQ section, ideally marked up with FAQPage schema.

E1.name: Listed in the site index
E1.why: Being indexed means AI data sources already know your site exists.
E1.fix: Keep the site reachable and crawlable so indexes can pick it up over time.

E2.name: AI-generated description
E2.why: This shows how AI currently summarises your site — your de-facto pitch to the models.
E2.fix: Sharpen your on-page copy so the AI summary reflects what you actually offer.

E3.name: Domain Rating
E3.why: Higher authority makes assistants more likely to trust and cite your pages.
E3.fix: Earn quality backlinks and publish authoritative, original content over time.

E4.name: Pages in the global index
E4.why: More indexed pages means more surface area for AI to find and cite.
E4.fix: Publish and interlink more crawlable pages, and submit your sitemap.

faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
faq.a1: It's optimizing your site so AI assistants and AI search can find, understand and cite it. Think of it as the AI-era counterpart to SEO.
faq.a2: An emerging plain-text file at your site root that tells AI models what your site is about and which pages matter — like robots.txt, but for describing content to LLMs.
faq.a3: Usually not. Blocking them means assistants can't read or cite you. Block specific bots only when you have a clear reason, such as protecting paid content.
faq.q4: Does a high score guarantee my site will be cited?
faq.a4: No. The score measures technical readiness. Whether you get cited also depends on content quality, authority and relevance. It's a guide, not a guarantee.
faq.a5: Our own live checks of your robots.txt, llms.txt, sitemap and homepage HTML, plus the free FreeSerp API for index presence and competitors.

method.title: Methodology
method.intro: CiteReady scores how ready a website is to be found, understood and cited by AI assistants and AI search. The score runs from 0 to 100 across five categories. Here is exactly what we check and how it adds up.
method.source1: Our own live checks: we fetch your robots.txt, llms.txt, sitemap.xml and homepage HTML directly from the server and analyse them.
method.source2: The free FreeSerp API: index presence, AI-generated description, Domain Rating and competitors in your niche.
method.scoring: Each check is Passed (full weight), Needs work (half), Missing (zero) or No data. A No-data check is excluded and its category is rescaled across the remaining checks, so missing third-party data never lowers your score.
method.disclaimer: This score is a diagnostic guide, not a guarantee. A high score improves your odds of being read and cited by AI, but actual citation also depends on content quality, authority and relevance, which no automated check can fully measure.
method.metaDesc: How CiteReady scores AI-readiness: every check, its weight, the data sources and what the score does and doesn't guarantee.
